Eye-tracking and EEG evidence further suggests that humans use holistic, intuitive, and flexible visual-cognitive processing to detect subtle inconsistencies and artifacts overlooked by AI. These findings clarify how humans and AI process deceptive visual cues differently and inform trustworthy, adaptive human-AI teaming for Deepfake detection.

item.title: The dynamic bodily self across lifespan: Agency, ownership, and the plasticity of internal body models
item.description:
Psychonomic Bulletin & Review
Two fundamental aspects of research on bodily self-consciousness, agency and body ownership, have recently seen exponential growth. The seminal paper of Botvinick and Cohen in 1998 provided a vital psychophysical tool for studying the bodily self - the rubber hand illusion, in which one feels as if an external object becomes a part of one's body. Recent motor control views of ownership highlight the influence of agency, the sense that one is in control of one's movements. Technological advancements have facilitated more ecologically valid experimental paradigms, such as virtual versions of the rubber hand illusion, furthering our understanding of the mechanisms through which the brain generates agency and ownership sensations. Recent findings suggest that agency and ownership can interact while remaining dissociable, as one may experience agency over an object that is not embodied or ownership of an object that cannot be controlled. Understanding the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying agency and ownership is critical for addressing the challenges of healthy aging. As sensory-motor precision declines across the lifespan, maintaining a coherent sense of body and control becomes essential for mobility, the successful adoption of assistive technologies, and overall cognitive resilience. This review synthesizes current findings on the agency-ownership interaction, discusses its neurobiological substrates, and explores its transformative potential for the design of "self-inclusive" prosthetics and brain-machine interfaces. We conclude by outlining a framework showing how optimization of these processes can support functional independence and psychological well-being in an aging population.

item.title: Lateralized amyloid PET uptake and beta-band connectivity in relation to cognition in temporal lobe epilepsy
item.description:
NeuroImage
We examined focus-relative amyloid PET asymmetry and its associations with resting-state EEG connectivity and processing speed in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy (MTLE). Thirty adults with clinically assigned MTLE (19 right-focus, 11 left-focus) underwent 18 F-florapronol PET and resting-state EEG. Regional standardized uptake value ratios (SUVRs) and sensor-level weighted phase lag index (wPLI) were evaluated using paired comparisons, rank correlations and exploratory bootstrap indirect-association models. Cognitive data were available for 26 participants, including Digit Symbol Coding (DSC) for 25. Under the original analytical convention, mean medial temporal SUVR was 1.066 ipsilaterally and 1.013 contralaterally (difference 0.053, 95% CI [0.013, 0.093]; p = 0.011; Cohen’s d z = 0.500). The contrast differed by focus side (interaction p = 0.002) and was 0.038 under source-table reconstruction ( p = 0.075). Ipsilateral SUVR correlated with inter-hemispheric beta wPLI ( ρ = 0.617, q = 0.034 across 240 tests). The intra-contralateral association ( ρ = 0.536) did not survive this broader correction. Indirect estimates for Trail Making Test A (0.279, 95% bootstrap CI [0.043, 0.761]) and DSC (0.151, 95% bootstrap CI [−0.114, 0.476]) did not survive correction across 136 models. Regional medial temporal PET uptake was associated with beta-band scalp connectivity in this small cohort, while focus-side heterogeneity and labeling sensitivity limit a uniform ipsilateral interpretation. Processing-speed indirect associations were exploratory and did not establish compensation or causality. Replication with structural correction, longer EEG sampling and longitudinal cognitive follow-up is required.

item.title: Validity and reliability of the Turkish version of the weight-related eating questionnaire in young adults
item.description:
BMC Psychology
This study aimed to adapt the Weight-Related Eating Questionnaire (WREQ) into Turkish and to evaluate its validity and reliability among young adults. The WREQ is a brief instrument assessing weight-related eating behaviors, including routine and compensatory restraint, susceptibility to external cues, and emotional eating. A total of 301 young adults aged 19–35 years from three regions of Türkiye participated. Translation and cultural adaptation of the WREQ followed International Test Commission guidelines. Construct validity was assessed using exploration factor analysis (EFA) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA). Convergent validity was examined through correlations with the Three-Factor Eating Questionnaire (TFEQ-R21) and the Dutch Eating Behaviour Questionnaire (DEBQ). Reliability was evaluated using Cronbach’s alpha, McDonald’s omega, and test–retest intraclass correlation coefficients. The sample consisted of 301 participants (85% female), with a mean age of 20.65 years (± 2.08) and a mean BMI of 22.33 kg/m² (± 3.67). EFA indicated adequate sampling adequacy (KMO = 0.88; Bartlett’s χ² = 2424.6, p < 0.001) and revealed a three-factor structure that explained 62.15% of the variance. The factors included Emotional Eating (33.96%), Dietary Restraint (19.32%), and Susceptibility to External Cues (8.87%), with communalities varying from 0.335 to 0.814. CFA indicated that the original four-factor model fit the data better than the three-factor model (Δχ²(3) = 41.025, p < 0.001; ΔCFI = 0.016), as shown by the following fit indices: χ ²/df = 2.46, RMSEA = 0.070, SRMR = 0.068, CFI = 0.940, and TLI = 0.920. Measurement invariance by sex was partially supported (ΔCFI ≤ 0.002). Convergent validity was evidenced by moderate to significant correlations with the TFEQ-R21 and DEBQ subscales ( r = 0.401–0.690, p < 0.001). BMI showed minor positive correlations with most subscales in the whole group. The overall scale exhibited strong internal consistency (α = 0.864), whereas subscales demonstrated acceptable to exceptional reliability (α = 0.708–0.924; ω = 0.725–0.927), HTMT readings below 0.85 corroborated discriminant validity. The Turkish version of the WREQ is a valid and reliable instrument for assessing weight-related eating behaviors among young adults and may serve as a useful tool in both research and clinical practice.

item.title: Assessing Extraneous and Intrinsic Cognitive Load of Teleoperation: A Physiological-Performance Study with Cognitive Load Theory
item.description:
International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
Teleoperation is critical in high-risk environments such as space missions, where operators face substantial cognitive demands.Existing studies often assessoverall cognitive load (CL) without distinguishing between intrinsic (ICL) and extraneous (ECL) components. This study examinedphysiological-performance correlates of ICL and ECL during space robotic arm teleoperations. A 2 × 2 experiment manipulated task difficulty (high/low) and operation mode (joystick/key), while measuring CL via subjective scales, attention allocation, electroencephalography (EEG) and pupil diameter. Results revealed that higher task difficulty significantly increased ICL, whereas joystick control elevated ECL. EEG spectral changes in frontal and occipital regions and pupil diameter variations provided complementary physiological evidence, but these measures should be regarded as exploratory correlates rather than validated source-specific biomarkers. These findings suggest that multimodal monitoring may support teleoperation interface design and adaptive assistance, while further validation is needed before physiological measures can reliably distinguish ICL and ECL.

item.title: Deep brain stimulation and spinal cord stimulation for chronic disorders of consciousness: a decade of clinical evidence, mechanistic insights, and critical appraisal
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Deep brain stimulation (DBS) and spinal cord stimulation (SCS) have been investigated for over four decades as neuromodulatory treatments for chronic disorders of consciousness (DOC), including the vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (VS/UWS) and the minimally conscious state (MCS), for which no disease-modifying pharmacological therapy exists. This narrative review synthesizes literature published between 2016 and 2026 on the neurobiological rationale, clinical evidence, neurophysiological biomarkers, and safety of DBS and SCS for chronic DOC. The 'mesocircuit hypothesis', supported by human intraoperative electrophysiology and nonhuman primate causal manipulation, provides a coherent rationale for central thalamic and centromedian-parafascicular targeting. Across case series, cohort studies, and individual patient data meta-analyses, both DBS and SCS produce clinically meaningful improvement in a minority of patients, consistently more often in MCS (63-74% response) than in VS/UWS (26-30% response), with younger age and shorter injury-to-treatment interval predicting better outcomes. However, the two largest individual patient data meta-analyses of DBS concur that current evidence is insufficient to conclude that stimulation alters the natural history of neurological recovery beyond what would be expected from patient selection and spontaneous recovery, and adverse event rates (8.1% for SCS, 18.2% for DBS) indicate non-trivial surgical risk in this vulnerable population. Neurophysiological and neuroimaging biomarkers derived from EEG, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, functional MRI, and FDG-PET show promise for objective outcome prediction but await prospective validation. We conclude that DBS and SCS remain experimental, mechanistically motivated but not yet definitively proven therapies for chronic DOC, and that adequately powered randomized controlled trials, biomarker-guided patient selection, and dedicated ethical frameworks are needed before either modality can be recommended outside of research settings.

item.title: Graded multisensory neurofeedback via the iNems system for comprehensive upper limb recovery after stroke: a multiple baseline study
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Introduction: Post-stroke upper-limb recovery remains challenging, especially in the presence of sensory impairments. Conventional brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are constrained by binary feedback, single-modality stimulation, and exclusion of patients with sensory deficits. We developed the Imagery Neurofeedback-based Multi-sensory System (iNems), a neurofeedback system that provides graded multisensory (visual and electrical) feedback based on ERD magnitude. This study validated iNems' efficacy in motor function, self-reported numbness, and cognitive functions using a multiple-baseline design (MBD). Methods: Four participants with post-stroke upper-limb motor and sensory impairments underwent a multiple baseline design. The baseline phase (phase A) used random feedback; the intervention (phase B) used adaptive iNems. iNems quantified motor intention via sensorimotor EEG event-related desynchronization (ERD) and delivered graded visual and electrical feedback. Primary outcomes were the Fugl-Meyer Assessment-Upper Extremity (FMA-UE) and Box and Block Test (BBT). Secondary outcomes included body cognition, numbness, and neurophysiological (ERD/ERS) changes. Results: All participants demonstrated significant improvement during the intervention. FMA-UE increased by 6-16 points. The BBT showed large effects (integrated Tau-U = 0.75). Body cognition improved significantly in both sense of agency (Tau-U = 0.80) and ownership (Tau-U = 0.89). Numbness was reduced in affected cases (Tau-U = -0.85). Neurophysiological changes correlated with functional gains, with some patterns suggesting increased neural efficiency. Conclusion: This first MBD-validated demonstration shows that graded, multisensory graded neurofeedback based on ERD magnitude can improve motor, self-reported numbness, and cognitive domains after stroke. These findings support adaptive closed-loop therapy as a promising, multifaceted rehabilitation strategy.

item.title: Reward positivity and affective functioning in early childhood: evidence from temporospatial principal components analysis
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Reward-related Positivity (RewP) indexes neural sensitivity to reward feedback and has been widely studied in adolescents and adults. However, little is known about how individual differences in RewP are associated with emotional functioning during early childhood, a critical period for affective development. Interpretation of feedback-related ERPs in children is further complicated by temporally overlapping components. This study examined whether a principal component analysis (PCA)-derived RewP is associated with affective functioning in children aged 4-7 years. Electroencephalography was recorded from 140 children during an age-appropriate reward task. Temporospatial PCA was performed on the full EEG sample ( n = 140), and primary regression analyses were conducted in the subset with complete covariate data ( n = 48). Temporospatial PCA was applied to isolate a RewP component differentiating gain from loss feedback. Positive and negative affect were assessed using the child version of the Positive and Negative Affect Schedule. Regression analyses examined whether PCA-derived RewP- and gain-related P200 amplitudes were associated with affective functioning while controlling for age, sex, ethnicity, income-to-need ratio, child depressive symptoms, and parental depressive symptoms. At the group level, boys showed greater PCA-derived gain-related P200 amplitudes than girls. At the individual level, higher child positive affect was associated with larger PCA-derived RewP amplitudes in the primary covariate-adjusted regression model. In sensitivity analyses conducted in the larger sample without the income-to-needs covariate, negative affect, rather than positive affect, was significantly associated with PCA-derived RewP amplitude. These findings provide novel evidence that RewP may serve as an early neural marker of affective functioning. By extending RewP research to an understudied developmental period and emphasizing normative emotional functioning, this study advances understanding of early reward processing and highlights the utility of PCA for isolating meaningful ERP components in children.

item.title: The gentle grip of beauty: Neural bases of motor inhibition during aesthetic appreciation
item.description:
Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience
A century-old tradition characterizes aesthetic experiences as intense contemplative moments in which we suspend practical concerns and devote our full attention to the object at hand. In line with this tradition, recent theories suggest that aesthetic experiences involve heightened sensory processing accompanied by a suppression of motor activity. Yet, while the link between aesthetic appreciation and perceptual enhancement has received considerable attention, the role of motor inhibition remains largely unexplored. The present study addressed this gap by investigating whether the aesthetic appreciation of images can modulate behavioral and electrophysiological markers of motor inhibition. In Experiment 1, significantly slower reaction times following the observation of preferred images were found. In Experiment 2, EEG responses associated with motor preparation and execution were significantly reduced in trials involving preferred compared with non-preferred images. Time-frequency analysis revealed significantly decreased alpha power (associated with attentional engagement toward visual perception) and increased beta power (associated with inhibited motor preparation) for preferred than non-preferred images. Overall, our results provide new evidence for the existence of a relationship between aesthetic appreciation and motor inhibition and position aesthetic experience as a valuable case study for exploring the adaptive coordination of sensory and motor systems in response to environmental demands.

item.title: From emotional inhibition to memory suppression: Acute exercise modulates electrophysiological dynamics associated with inhibitory control during suppression of negative memories
item.description:
International Journal of Psychophysiology
Failures in inhibitory control over negative emotional memories can lead to intrusive recollections that interfere with cognitive functioning and well-being. The present study examined whether acute exercise modulates the electrophysiological dynamics underlying inhibitory control during the suppression of negative emotional memories. Seventy healthy participants were randomly assigned to an acute exercise group or a seated-rest control group. The exercise group completed 30 min of moderate-intensity exercise, whereas the control group remained seated at rest. Participants completed the emotional Think/No-Think paradigm both before and after the intervention, while electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded. Event-related potentials (ERPs), time-frequency analyses, and multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) were used to characterize neural processes associated with inhibitory control. Results showed that acute exercise selectively modulated late-stage neural activity during negative memory suppression, particularly within the 2400-3000 ms time window. This modulation was most evident over central site and left parietal site, and was accompanied by changes in alpha- and beta-band power at the left parieto-occipital junction. Overall, these findings suggest that acute exercise modulates late-stage neural dynamics during the suppression of negative memories. The observed neural changes were accompanied by a reduction in intrusion frequency during suppression attempts, consistent with the possibility that acute exercise facilitates late-stage sustained inhibition.

item.title: Recall of overlearned speech in noise: Developmental ERP findings and an episodic buffer frame for culturally situated brain activity
item.description:
Brain and Cognition
How does extensively practiced speech memory remain dependent on momentary sensory input, and how does this interaction shape brain activity during development? This perspective integrates exploratory behavioral and event-related potential (ERP) findings from a culturally situated spoken-sequence recognition paradigm with a working memory episodic-buffer account. We reanalyzed data from children and young adults who had memorized Quranic passages despite limited Arabic comprehension. Participants heard incomplete passages with or without static noise and selected the missing final word from phonologically plausible alternatives. Noise reduced recognition accuracy, and children generally responded more slowly. Descriptive ERP patterns revealed larger, more spatially distributed responses in children, spanning early auditory processing, mid-latency positivity, and later negative activity. We propose that recognition requires temporary binding of acoustic input, serial and rhythmic expectations, visual response cues, and consolidated sequence knowledge within an episodic buffer under executive control. Noise may impair perceptual fidelity and matching between transient input and stored representations. Developmental ERP differences may reflect representational coordination rather than neural efficiency. These preliminary findings motivate testable predictions concerning cross-modal congruence, familiarity, comprehension, and independently measured expertise. Culturally embedded learning practices provide informative contexts for examining interactions among working memory, long-term knowledge, and developing neural systems supporting cognition.

item.title: Experiential avoidance and smartphone addiction in adolescents: a study using multi-model machine learning and mediation analysis
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background: Smartphone addiction is closely associated with adolescents' mental health and educational outcomes. Current research lacks comprehensive machine learning studies for predicting smartphone addiction factors, and studies examining relationships between various factors including mediation effects are also insufficient. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 3,405 adolescents in China (1,853 boys, 54.4%; 1,552 girls, 45.6%; mean age = 14.50 years, SD = 1.18). Eight machine learning algorithms (Linear Regression, Ridge Regression, Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Support Vector Regression, Bayesian Ridge Regression) were employed with SHAP analysis for interpretability. Predictive variables included demographic characteristics, social support, experiential avoidance, self-efficacy, and emotional symptoms. Baron and Kenny's method was used for mediation effect analysis. Results: = 0.478, RMSE = 8.66). SHAP analysis identified experiential avoidance as the strongest predictor (SHAP value = 5.472), followed by depressive symptoms (1.723), BMI category (1.438), age (1.394), and anxiety symptoms (1.337). Mediation analysis revealed that social support's negative association with smartphone addiction (total effect = -0.231) was almost indirect (-0.252), with experiential avoidance mediating the majority of the total effect. The final model explained 49.4% of variance in smartphone addiction. Conclusion: Experiential avoidance is a strong correlate of adolescent smartphone addiction and plays a mediating role in the association between social support and smartphone addiction. This finding is consistent with the "reality deficit-virtual compensation" theoretical framework. Additionally, depressive symptoms, BMI category, age, and anxiety symptoms were also independently associated with smartphone addiction.

item.title: Behavioural expression of ictal embarrassment: a stereo-EEG case report
item.description:
Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
Embarrassment is a rare ictal manifestation whose neurophysiological basis remains poorly understood. We describe the case of a 40-year-old woman with drug-resistant focal epilepsy characterized by an unusual ictal semiology combining an intense positive emotional experience with behavioral manifestations of embarrassment. Stereo-EEG demonstrated seizure onset within the middle frontal gyrus bank of the superior frontal sulcus (F2sb), with rapid propagation to the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC) and superior anterior insula (sAI). Electrical stimulation of the F2sb reliably reproduced the habitual electroclinical seizure. While identical stimulation parameters elicited the subjective and autonomic manifestations in both supine and upright postures, the complete behavioral repertoire of embarrassment emerged only when stimulation was delivered in the standing position. Exploratory functional connectivity analyses revealed that overt embarrassment was associated with reduced node strength within a network encompassing the dACC, sAI, mesial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC). More restricted network changes were associated with only mild sensations, whereas asymptomatic stimulation produced a distinct and partly reversed connectivity pattern. This case suggests that the behavioral expression of ictal embarrassment arises from the transient reconfiguration of a frontal-cingulo-insular network and is critically shaped by bodily context.

item.title: Neural Representations of Perceptual Reorganization in the Musical Scale Illusion
item.description:
Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
The auditory system organizes complex acoustic input into coherent perceptual streams, yet how neural responses relate to physical stimulus structure and reported perception when the two diverge remains unclear. We investigated perceptual reorganization using the scale illusion, in which interleaved tone sequences presented separately to the two ears are typically heard as continuous melodic streams.Thirty participants listened to illusory, zigzag, and continuous sequences during EEG recording and reported whether each sequence sounded continuous or zigzag. Temporal response function models characterized neural encoding and reconstruction of amplitude-envelope (envelope) and pitch-change magnitude features. We tested whether neural responses during illusory listening corresponded more closely to reference patterns associated with the physical zigzag structure or reported continuous organization. Illusory sequences were predominantly categorized as Continuous and elicited longer RTs than non-illusory sequences. Encoding models revealed delayed pitch-change magnitude responses in the illusory condition, whereas envelope latencies remained comparatively stable. For pitch-change magnitude, reconstruction correlations computed over the full sequence exceeded chance levels estimated separately for each reference, with higher correlations for the continuous reference. Envelope correlations exceeded neither chance level, despite a small relative preference for the zigzag reference. These findings show that neural response timing and relative correspondence with the tested reference patterns depend on the modeled feature during the scale illusion. The reconstruction result concerns correlations across complete sequences and does not establish continuous tracking of the perceived melody.

item.title: No added benefit of VR and neurofeedback-enhanced VR for trait mindfulness in long-term mindfulness training
item.description:
Computers in Human Behavior Reports
Immersive virtual reality (VR) and neurofeedback (NF) are increasingly promoted to enhance mindfulness meditation, yet it remains unknown whether these externally engaging technologies confer lasting benefits for trait mindfulness over sustained practice. This longitudinal randomized controlled trial compared three conditions over a 4-week program (eight sessions) with a three-month follow-up: screen-based audio-guided mindfulness (Non-VR), mindfulness in an immersive VR environment (VR), and mindfulness in VR with real-time EEG neurofeedback (VR-NF). Ninety-four meditation-naïve participants completed the study. Trait mindfulness (Five Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire, FFMQ) was assessed at six time points, EEG signal was recorded during all sessions, and subjective presence (Igroup Presence Questionnaire, IPQ) in VR was measured. Linear mixed models and Bayesian analysis revealed comparable FFMQ increases across all three groups, indicating that VR and VR-NF did not confer added behavioral benefit for trait mindfulness development. Higher IPQ presence scores showed a modest negative correlation with long-term FFMQ gains at three-month follow-up. Exploratory EEG analyses described a numerically steeper theta trajectory in the Non-VR group relative to the VR and VR-NF groups, whereas alpha trajectories were comparable across groups. However, because the two EEG systems were not equivalent across conditions and recordings were obtained from frontopolar sites, these patterns are descriptive only and cannot be interpreted as evidence of group differences. Taken together, these findings suggest that VR and VR-NF did not confer added benefit for trait mindfulness in long-term mindfulness training.

item.title: Lifestyles, psychological well-being, and mental health: A cross-sectional study in a higher education sample
item.description:
BMC Psychology
Abstract Background The transition to higher education represents a critical developmental stage during which lifestyle behaviours and psychosocial factors interact to influence well-being and mental health. Understanding these dynamics is essential to prevent adverse health outcomes and support academic success. This study aimed to (i) describe lifestyle patterns among Portuguese higher education students, (ii) examine their associations with well-being and mental health, and (iii) assess the influence of sociodemographic and contextual variables. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted with 1,159 students from the Polytechnic of Porto, Portugal. Participants completed the FANTASTICO Lifestyle Questionnaire, the Depression, Anxiety and Stress Scale (DASS-21), and the CORE-18 to assess lifestyle behaviours and mental health indicators. Descriptive analyses were performed, and one-way ANOVA and independent Student’s t-tests were used to compare lifestyle and psychological variables across sociodemographic groups. Pearson’s correlation coefficients were calculated to examine associations with age, body mass index (BMI), and self-rated health. A multiple linear regression model using a stepwise method identified explanatory variables of lifestyle scores. Results The mean age of the sample was 21.51 (± 2.65) years; most participants were women (69.70%) and lived with their families (71.00%). Students reported overall favourable lifestyle profiles and relatively low psychological distress. However, mild symptoms of depression, anxiety, and stress were present, approaching the threshold for moderate severity. Higher self-rated health, absence of depressive symptoms, lower stress levels, lower BMI, female gender, younger age, and enrolment in the School of Health Sciences were significantly associated with healthier lifestyle scores. Fourth-year students also reported better lifestyle and mental health indicators than those in earlier years. An unexpected positive association emerged between the CORE-18 problems/symptoms subscale and lifestyle scores, possibly reflecting compensatory health behaviours among students more aware of psychological symptoms. Conclusions These findings highlight the complex interplay between psychological well-being, lifestyle, and sociodemographic factors in higher education students. Future research should include more diverse samples, consider additional factors such as social support, economic pressures, and physical context, and adopt longitudinal designs with objective measures to better capture the relationships between lifestyle and mental health.

item.title: Real-time fMRI neurofeedback of left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex to enhance emotional cognitive control: A randomized controlled trial
item.description:
NeuroImage
Real-time fMRI neurofeedback (rt-fMRI-nf) is an endogenous neuromodulation approach whereby individuals are taught to self-regulate their own neural activity in the moment. Cognitive control in emotional contexts is related to risk for or protection against mental health disorders, such as depression, anxiety, or posttraumatic stress disorder. The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) has been shown to be centrally important in facilitating emotional cognitive control (ECC). Using a double-blind randomized controlled trial design, the present study tested a novel rt-fMRI-nf protocol to increase left dlPFC activity during ECC and improve ECC measured by self-report and behavioral task performance. Seventy healthy adult participants were enrolled and randomized to either active (n = 37; left dlPFC) or sham [n = 33; left postcentral gyrus (PCG)] neurofeedback. Linear mixed effects models tested for effects of time (practice/run 1/run 2/run 3/transfer), feedback target (active/sham), and their interaction on left dlPFC activity, left PCG activity, and ECC measures (self-report and behavior). Results showed a significant time-by-feedback interaction on left dlPFC activity (p = .031). This interaction was such that active feedback led to greater left dlPFC activity in run 1 (p = .030; d = .66) and run 2 (p = .042; d = .62), but not for run 3 nor the transfer run (when no feedback was provided). There were no significant effects of feedback on ECC measures. These findings demonstrate that rt-fMRI-nf had an initial but not a sustained effect on left dlPFC activity, providing evidence of neural target engagement. However, the lack of a sustained effect on neural activity nor any observed effects on ECC highlight the complexity of identifying the optimal design and dosing for novel rt-fMRI-nf protocols.

item.title: Short-term responses across two sequential plant-based activity sessions: an exploratory fixed-order pilot study
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Structured plant-based activities combine natural materials, purposeful manual work, sensory engagement, and social interaction, but direct comparisons of practical formats in community adults remain limited. We characterized short-term responses during two sequential sessions and compared within-session changes. Methods Twenty-five adults participated in a single-group, fixed-order pilot study. Session 1 involved horticultural crafting; 1 week later, Session 2 involved balm crafting followed by horticultural crafting. Twenty-three attended both sessions. DASS-21 and STAI-S were principal outcomes; horticultural wellbeing, HRV, and forehead single-channel EEG were exploratory. Within-session changes and complete-case between-session differences were estimated with 95% CIs. Post hoc TOST examined exploratory equivalence bounds. Results Both sessions were followed by favorable short-term psychological changes. DASS-21 scores decreased by 8.57 points in Session 1 [95% CI (5.41, 11.72), n = 23] and 5.53 in Session 2 [(2.65, 8.41), n = 17]. STAI-S scores decreased by 7.30 points in Session 1 [(5.23, 9.37), n = 25] and 6.86 in Session 2 [(4.07, 9.66), n = 22]; all four Holm-adjusted p values were <0.001. Complete-case comparisons showed no statistically detectable between-session difference in DASS-21 improvement [3.12 points, 95% CI (−1.51, 7.75)] or STAI-S improvement [0.34 points, (−3.15, 3.83)]. STAI-S changes met the exploratory TOST criterion only at the broad ±0.50 standardized bound. Horticultural wellbeing improved in both sessions; SDNN and RMSSD increased, whereas EEG findings did not remain significant after multiplicity correction. Conclusion Both sessions were associated with favorable short-term psychological changes, particularly reduced distress and state anxiety. These findings support the feasibility and potential value of brief, hands-on plant-based activities in community settings and provide estimates for larger randomized, counterbalanced trials. Given the fixed order and absence of a control group, the findings are preliminary rather than definitive causal or modality-specific evidence.

item.title: Body image and maladaptive eating behaviors in Chinese early adolescents: a latent profile analysis
item.description:
Frontiers in Psychology
Background Body image undergoes significant changes during early adolescence, yet empirical evidence on how the combination of negative and positive body image in this stage relates to maladaptive eating behaviors remains limited. To address this, employing a person-centered approach, this study aimed to identify distinct profiles of body image and to explore the relationships between profile membership, gender, body mass index (BMI), socioeconomic status (SES), and maladaptive eating behaviors among Chinese early adolescents. Methods Using indicators from three dimensions of positive body image (i.e., body self-appreciation, body other-appreciation, resilience against negative appearance feedback) and negative body image (i.e., body dissatisfaction), latent profile analysis (LPA) was conducted with a sample of 1,248 junior high school students (aged 12–15 years, M = 13.42, SD = 1.03; 50.4% boys) from Heilongjiang Province, China. Results Three distinct body image profiles were identified: the Positive Body Image Group (66.59%), the Body Other-Appreciation Dominant Group (23.88%), and the Moderate Body Image Group (9.54%). Gender and BMI significantly predicted profile membership, whereas SES did not. Regarding maladaptive eating behaviors, both the Body Other-Appreciation Dominant Group and the Moderate Body Image Group reported significantly higher levels of restrained eating than the Positive Body Image Group. The Moderate Body Image Group also reported significantly higher levels of emotional eating compared with the Positive Body Image Group. No significant differences were found in external eating among the three profiles. Conclusion Early adolescents' body image profiles exhibit significant heterogeneity, with distinct patterns of association with maladaptive eating behaviors across profiles. Accordingly, interventions should consider gender and body mass index and be tailored to the characteristics of each profile to improve body image and eating behaviors.
